relationship: parallel dreams associated with folly and futility
rationale: Sirach joins foolish hopes with dreams; Ecclesiastes likewise connects dreams with distraction and futilities, concluding with fear of God.
source_text: Empty and false hopes belong to a man without understanding, and dreams give wings to fools.

target_units.text: For a dream comes with much distraction, and a fool’s voice with many words.
Whenever you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for there is no delight in fools. Pay whatever you vow.
Better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay.
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before God, “It was ignorance,” lest God become angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands.
For with many dreams come futilities and many words; therefore fear God.

relationship: parallel futility of relying on dreams
rationale: Sirach compares reliance on dreams with grasping a shadow; Zechariah calls false dreams vain comfort, without repeating the shadow image.
source_text: Like someone grasping a shadow and chasing wind is the one who relies on dreams.

target_units.text: For those making pronouncements spoke troubles, the diviners false visions; they were telling false dreams and giving vain comfort. Therefore they were carried away like sheep and mistreated, because there was no healing.

relationship: close question about cleanness from uncleanness
rationale: Both ask how cleanness can arise from uncleanness; Sirach adds the analogous question about truth coming from falsehood.
source_text: What will be cleansed from something unclean? What will prove true from something false?

target_units.text: For who will be clean from filth? No one.

relationship: parallel rejection of divination and omens
rationale: Sirach calls divinations and omens vain; Deuteronomy forbids Israel to follow those practices. The laboring-woman image belongs to Sirach.
source_text: Divinations, omens, and dreams are vain, and the heart imagines like a woman in labor.

target_units.text: There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter by fire, or practises divination, or interprets spoken omens, or observes auguries, or works sorcery,
or chants spells, or is a medium, or observes portents, or inquires of the dead.
For everyone who does these things is an abomination unto the Lord your God; for because of these abominations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.
You shall be perfect before the Lord your God.
For these nations whose possession you inherit hearken unto omens and divinations; but the Lord your God has not granted you so to do.

relationship: qualifying parallel of divinely given dreams
rationale: Sirach excepts dreams sent by the Most High from its warning; Numbers explicitly allows divine speech through prophetic sleep, distinguishing Moses's manner of revelation.
source_text: Unless they are sent from the Most High in a visitation, do not give your heart to them.

target_units.text: And He said unto them: Hear My words: If there is a prophet among you unto the Lord, I will make Myself known unto him in a vision, and I will speak unto him in sleep.
Not so My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house.
I will speak unto him mouth to mouth, in visible appearance, and not through riddles; and he saw the glory of the Lord. And why were you not afraid to speak against My servant Moses?

relationship: close warning that false dreams lead people astray
rationale: Sirach says reliance on dreams has led many astray; Jeremiah describes unsent prophets leading God's people astray through false dreams.
source_text: For dreams have led many astray, and those who hoped in them fell away.

target_units.text: I heard what the prophets speak, the false things they prophesy in My name, saying, I dreamed a dream.
How long will it be in the heart of the prophets prophesying false things, and in their prophesying the wishes of their own heart?
They plan to forget My law through their dreams, which each told his neighbor, just as their fathers forgot My name through Baal.
Let the prophet in whom there is a dream tell his dream, and the one to whom My word comes tell My word in truth. What has chaff to do with wheat? So are My words, says the Lord.
Are not My words like blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe cutting rock?
Therefore behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord God, who steal My words, each from his neighbor.
Behold, I am against the prophets who cast out prophecies of the tongue and doze their own dozing.

Behold, I am against the prophets who prophesy false dreams, who told them and led My people astray by their lies and wanderings. I did not send or command them, and they will bring this people no benefit at all.

relationship: parallel assurance of the law's fulfillment
rationale: Sirach says the law will be fulfilled without falsehood; Jesus likewise denies its abolition and affirms fulfillment, with His own role expressly stated.
source_text: The law will be fulfilled without falsehood, and wisdom is fulfillment in a faithful mouth.

target_units.text: Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish, but to fulfil.
For truly I tell you: until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota nor one stroke shall pass from the Law, until all things come to pass.

relationship: related learning through travel and human experience
rationale: Sirach 34 associates wandering with acquired understanding; 39:4 likewise joins foreign travel with experience of good and evil among people.
source_text: A man who has wandered has learned much, and one with much experience will recount understanding.

target_units.text: He will serve among dignitaries and appear before rulers. He will pass through the land of foreign nations, for he has experienced good and evil among human beings.

relationship: related learning through undergone experience
rationale: Sirach contrasts the untested person's limited knowledge with experience; Hebrews gives the distinct case of the Son learning obedience through suffering. Sirach concerns practical skill; Hebrews specifically names obedience.
source_text: The one who has not been tested knows little, but the one who has wandered will increase in skill.

target_units.text: Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from the things He suffered,

relationship: parallel survival after danger approaching death
rationale: Both speakers recall danger approaching death and preservation. Paul expressly identifies God as deliverer; Sirach leaves the preserving agency unnamed within its account of experience.
source_text: Often I was in danger to the point of death, and because of these things I was preserved.

target_units.text: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of our affliction that occurred in Asia: we were burdened far beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of living.
Indeed, we ourselves had the sentence of death within us, so that we might rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
He delivered us from so great a death and will deliver us; in Him we have set our hope that He will deliver us yet again,

relationship: close fear of God joined with saving hope
rationale: Sirach joins fear of the Lord, life and hope in the Savior; the psalm similarly joins fear, hope, rescue from death and divine help.
source_text: The spirit of those who fear the Lord will live, for their hope rests upon the One who saves them.

target_units.text: Behold, the Lord’s eyes are upon those who fear Him, those who hope in His mercy,
to rescue their souls from death and nourish them in famine.
Our soul waits for the Lord, for He is our helper and defender.
For our heart will rejoice in Him, and we have hoped in His holy name.
May Thy mercy, Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in Thee.

relationship: close freedom from fear through divine protection
rationale: Both deny the need for fear because the Lord protects and saves; both explicitly place hope in Him amid danger.
source_text: The one who fears the Lord will fear nothing and certainly not be cowardly, because He Himself is his hope.

target_units.text: Of David, before being anointed. The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom will I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom will I be afraid?
When those doing evil approached me to eat my flesh, those who afflict me and my enemies, they grew weak and fell.
Even if an army draws up against me, my heart will not fear; even if war rises against me, in this I hope.

relationship: close blessedness of the God-fearing person
rationale: Sirach calls the God-fearing soul happy and asks about its support; the psalm calls that person blessed and describes a heart established in hope.
source_text: Happy is the soul of the one who fears the Lord! On whom does he rely? Who is his support?

target_units.text: Hallelujah! Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in His commandments.
His seed will be powerful in the land; a generation of the upright will be blessed.
Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness remains for an age of an age.
Light sprang up in darkness for the upright— merciful, compassionate and righteous.
Kind is the man who has compassion and lends; he will manage his words with judgment.
For he will never be shaken; the righteous person will be an everlasting memorial.
He will not fear an evil report; his heart is ready to hope in the Lord.
His heart is established; he shall certainly not fear, until he looks upon his enemies.

relationship: close divine eyes and protective support
rationale: Sirach places God's eyes upon those who love Him and calls Him shield and support; the psalm similarly joins His attentive eyes with help and defense.
source_text: The Lord’s eyes are upon those who love Him: a mighty shield and strong support, shelter from scorching heat and shelter from midday, protection from stumbling and help against falling,

target_units.text: Behold, the Lord’s eyes are upon those who fear Him, those who hope in His mercy,
to rescue their souls from death and nourish them in famine.
Our soul waits for the Lord, for He is our helper and defender.

relationship: close protection from stumbling and scorching sun
rationale: Both combine protection of the person's footing with divine shelter against the sun's heat, beyond their general language of help.
source_text: The Lord’s eyes are upon those who love Him: a mighty shield and strong support, shelter from scorching heat and shelter from midday, protection from stumbling and help against falling,

target_units.text: Do not give your foot over to shaking, and may your Keeper not slumber.
Behold, the One guarding Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
The Lord will guard you; the Lord is your shelter at your right hand.
By day the sun will not scorch you, nor the moon by night.

relationship: parallel divine healing and renewal of life
rationale: Sirach attributes healing, life and blessing to God; the psalm likewise blesses Him for healing, redeeming life and renewing youth. Brightened eyes are Sirach's additional image.
source_text: raising the soul and brightening the eyes, giving healing, life, and blessing.

target_units.text: Of David. Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, His holy name.
Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all His repayments:
who is gracious toward all your lawless deeds, who heals all your diseases;
who redeems your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassions;
who fills your desire with good things; your youth will be renewed like an eagle’s.

relationship: close rejection of unjustly acquired and blemished offerings
rationale: Sirach calls sacrifice from unjust gain blemished and unacceptable; Malachi likewise questions acceptance of things seized by force and damaged sacrificial animals.
source_text: One who sacrifices from unjust gain makes a blemished offering, and the gifts of the lawless bring no acceptance.

target_units.text: “And you said, ‘These things are from hardship,’ and I blew them away,” says the Lord Almighty. “You were bringing things seized by force, the lame and the afflicted. If you bring the sacrifice, shall I accept these things from your hands?” says the Lord Almighty.

“Cursed is one who was able, and had a male in his flock and a vow concerning it, yet sacrifices a damaged animal to the Lord. For I am a great King,” says the Lord Almighty, “and My name is manifest among the nations.”

relationship: close rejection of multiplied sacrifices without repentance
rationale: Sirach denies that many sacrifices atone for the ungodly; Isaiah likewise rejects a multitude of offerings from bloodstained worshippers and commands cleansing from evil.
source_text: The Most High takes no pleasure in the offerings of the ungodly, nor does He atone for sins through a multitude of sacrifices.

target_units.text: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me?” says the Lord. “I am full of burnt offerings of rams; fat of lambs and blood of bulls and male goats I do not desire,
not even if you come to appear before Me. For who demanded these things from your hands? To trample My court,
you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,
and your new moons and your festivals My soul hates. You have become more than enough for Me; I will no longer let your sins go.
Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.
Wash yourselves, become clean. Remove the evils from your souls, before My eyes. Stop your evil deeds.

relationship: related sacrificial worship joined with bloodguilt
rationale: Sirach likens sacrifice from poor people's property to killing a son before his father; Isaiah also joins rejected sacrifice with blood-filled hands, without Sirach's particular comparison.
source_text: The one who presents a sacrifice from the property of the poor is slaughtering a son before his father.

target_units.text: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me?” says the Lord. “I am full of burnt offerings of rams; fat of lambs and blood of bulls and male goats I do not desire,
not even if you come to appear before Me. For who demanded these things from your hands? To trample My court,
you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,
and your new moons and your festivals My soul hates. You have become more than enough for Me; I will no longer let your sins go.
Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

relationship: parallel taking life-sustaining food from the vulnerable
rationale: Sirach condemns depriving poor people of bread as bloodshed; Job likewise describes oppressors taking the hungry person's morsel, without that explicit homicide designation.
source_text: The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; the one who deprives them of it is a man of blood.

target_units.text: They snatched an orphan from the breast and humbled one who had fallen.
They unjustly made people lie down naked and took the morsel from the hungry.

relationship: close withheld wages linked with bloodguilt
rationale: Sirach calls withholding wages bloodshed; James likewise joins withheld harvesters' wages, their cries, and the charge of murdering the righteous.
source_text: The one who takes away a livelihood murders his neighbor, and the one who withholds a hired worker’s wage sheds blood.

target_units.text: Look, the wages of the laborers who reaped your fields, withheld by you, cry out; and the cries of the harvesters have entered the ears of the Lord Sabaoth.
You lived luxuriously on the earth and indulged yourselves; you fattened your hearts on a day of slaughter.
You condemned; you murdered the righteous one. He does not oppose you.

relationship: legal counterpart prohibiting withheld wages
rationale: Sirach describes withholding wages as bloodshed; Leviticus supplies the concrete command against retaining a hired worker's wages overnight, alongside prohibitions of robbery and wronging a neighbor.
source_text: The one who takes away a livelihood murders his neighbor, and the one who withholds a hired worker’s wage sheds blood.

target_units.text: You shall not wrong your neighbour, neither shall you rob; and the wages of the hired worker shall in no wise remain with you overnight until morning.

relationship: related opposing acts of building and demolition
rationale: Sirach pictures one person's building undone by another; Paul pictures himself rebuilding what he demolished. Both use opposing construction acts negatively, for different stated reasons.
source_text: One builds and another tears down; what have they gained beyond toil?

target_units.text: For if I rebuild the things I tore down, I show myself to be a transgressor.

relationship: related opposition between prayerful speech and cursing
rationale: Sirach questions the outcome when one prays and another curses; James rejects blessing God and cursing people from the same mouth. The number of speakers differs.
source_text: One prays and another curses; whose voice will the Master hear?

target_units.text: With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings who have been made in God’s likeness.
From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to happen this way.

relationship: legal background of corpse-contact impurity
rationale: Sirach's washing-and-retouching example depends on corpse contact causing impurity; Numbers explicitly prescribes purification after such contact, explaining the example's renewed defilement.
source_text: Someone washes after contact with a corpse and then touches it again; what has he gained by his washing?

target_units.text: Whosoever touches a dead person, any human being who has died, shall be unclean for seven days.
That person shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh day, and he shall be clean. If he is not purified on the third day and on the seventh day, he shall not be clean.

Whosoever touches the dead body of any human being who has died, and is not purified, has defiled the Tent of the Lord; that soul shall be wiped out from Israel. Because water of sprinkling was not sprinkled upon him, he is unclean; his uncleanness is still in him.

relationship: close return to defilement after cleansing
rationale: Sirach compares repeated sin after fasting with renewed corpse defilement; Peter likewise condemns return after escape and uses the washed sow returning to mud.
source_text: So is a person who fasts over his sins and goes again to do the same things. Who will hear his prayer, and what has he gained by humbling himself?

target_units.text: For if, after escaping the world’s defilements through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their last state has become worse than their first.
For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them.
What the true proverb says has happened to them: “A dog has returned to its own vomit,” and, “A sow, after washing, returns to wallowing in mud.”

relationship: close fasting contradicted by continuing injustice
rationale: Both question fasting's benefit when wrongful conduct continues; Isaiah specifies oppression and violence and connects corrected conduct with prayer being heard.
source_text: So is a person who fasts over his sins and goes again to do the same things. Who will hear his prayer, and what has he gained by humbling himself?

target_units.text: saying, ‘Why did we fast, and Thou didst not see? We humbled our lives, and Thou didst not notice?’ For on your fasting days you pursue your wishes and prod all those under your control.
If you fast for lawsuits and fights and strike a humble person with fists, why do you fast for Me as today, to make your voice heard in an outcry?

I did not choose this fast, or a day for a person to humble his life. Even if you bend your neck like a ring and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you, you will not thereby call it an acceptable fast.

‘It is not such a fast that I chose,’ says the Lord. ‘Instead, loosen every bond of injustice, undo the strangling ties of coercive agreements, release the crushed, and tear up every unjust written contract.
Break your bread for the hungry and bring homeless poor people into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; do not overlook those belonging to your own family.
Then your light will break out early, and your healings quickly rise. Your righteousness will go ahead of you, and God’s glory will enfold you.
Then you will cry, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking He will say, “Behold, I am present.” If you remove from yourself a bond, finger-pointing, and a word of grumbling,

relationship: related obedience valued in relation to sacrifice
rationale: Sirach describes keeping commandments as sacrificial offering; Samuel declares obedience and attentiveness better than sacrifice, expressing a different relationship between conduct and ritual.
source_text: The one who keeps the law multiplies offerings; the one who attends to commandments sacrifices a peace offering.

target_units.text: Samuel said, “Are whole burnt offerings and sacrifices as desirable to the Lord as listening to the Lord’s voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness than the fat of rams.

relationship: close beneficence described as sacrifice
rationale: Sirach calls kindness and almsgiving offerings; Hebrews similarly calls doing good and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God, alongside sacrifice of praise.
source_text: The one who repays kindness offers fine flour, and the one who gives alms sacrifices a praise offering.

target_units.text: Therefore through Him let us continually offer God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing His name.
And do not forget to do good and to share, for God is pleased with such sacrifices.

relationship: close repentance associated with forgiveness and divine pleasure
rationale: Sirach calls withdrawal from wickedness God's pleasure and withdrawal from injustice atonement; Ezekiel likewise joins turning from lawlessness with forgotten transgressions and God's desire for the person's life.
source_text: To withdraw from wickedness is the Lord’s good pleasure, and to withdraw from injustice is atonement.

target_units.text: If the lawless person turns from all the lawlessness he committed, keeps all My commandments, and practices righteousness and mercy, he will surely live; he certainly will not die.
None of the transgressions he committed will be remembered. By the righteousness he practiced, he will live.
Do I at all desire the death of the lawless, says the Lord, rather than his turning from his evil way and living?

relationship: close prohibition of appearing empty before God
rationale: Sirach repeats the requirement not to appear empty before the Lord; Exodus states that requirement within the prescribed feast observance.
source_text: Do not appear empty before the Lord, for all these things are for the commandment’s sake.

target_units.text: Keep the feast of unleavened bread; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time in the month of new grain; for in it you came out of Egypt. You shall not appear before Me empty-handed.

relationship: close pleasing sacrifice and fragrant aroma
rationale: Sirach describes a righteous offering's fragrance before God; Paul likewise calls the Philippians' material gift a fragrant aroma and acceptable sacrifice.
source_text: A righteous person’s offering fattens the altar, and its fragrance is before the Most High.

target_units.text: But I have received everything and have an abundance; I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things from you, a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God.

relationship: related righteous giving remembered before God
rationale: Sirach promises an acceptable offering an unforgettable memorial; the angel describes Cornelius's alms and prayers as a memorial ascending before God.
source_text: A righteous man’s sacrifice is acceptable, and its memorial will not be forgotten.

target_units.text: devout and fearing God with his whole household, giving many alms to the people and praying to God continually.
About the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God come in to him and say, “Cornelius.”
He stared at him in fear and said, “What is it, sir?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.

relationship: close honoring God with firstfruits
rationale: Both command honoring the Lord through firstfruits; Sirach emphasizes generous giving without diminishing them, while Proverbs specifies righteous labors and resulting abundance.
source_text: Glorify the Lord with a generous eye, and do not diminish the firstfruits of your hands.

target_units.text: Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and offer Him firstfruits from your fruits of righteousness,
so that your storerooms may be filled with an abundance of grain and your vats gush with wine.

relationship: close cheerful disposition in giving
rationale: Sirach commands a cheerful face and gladness with gifts and tithes; Paul likewise commends cheerful giving without sorrow or compulsion, without specifying a tithe.
source_text: With every gift make your face cheerful, and consecrate a tenth with gladness.

target_units.text: Let each give as he has decided in his heart, not out of sorrow or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.

relationship: related tithe observance joined with rejoicing
rationale: Sirach specifically joins consecrating a tenth with gladness; Deuteronomy prescribes the tithe and its observance before God with the household's rejoicing.
source_text: With every gift make your face cheerful, and consecrate a tenth with gladness.

target_units.text: You shall surely tithe all the produce of your seed, the yield of your field, year by year.

And you shall eat it before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord your God shall choose for His name to be called upon there. You shall bring the tithes of your grain, and of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your cattle and of your sheep, that you may learn to fear the Lord your God all your days.

And if the way is too long for you, so that you cannot carry them, because the place which the Lord your God shall choose for His name to be called upon there is far from you, when the Lord your God has blessed you,
then you shall sell them for silver, and take the silver in your hands, and go unto the place which the Lord your God shall choose.

And you shall spend the silver for whatsoever your soul desires, for cattle, or for sheep, or for wine, or for strong drink, or for whatsoever your soul desires; and you shall eat there before the Lord your God, and rejoice, you and your house,

relationship: close giving measured by God's gift and human ability
rationale: Both measure the worshipper's gift by what the hand can provide and the blessing already received from God.
source_text: Give to the Most High according to His gift, with a generous eye according to what your hand has found.

target_units.text: but every man according to the ability of your hands, according to the blessing of the Lord your God which He has given you.

relationship: parallel divine repayment of generosity
rationale: Both promise that God repays giving; Proverbs specifies mercy to the poor, while Sirach adds the sevenfold description.
source_text: For the Lord repays, and He will repay you sevenfold.

target_units.text: One who has mercy on the poor lends to God, and He will repay him according to his gift.

relationship: close divine refusal of bribes
rationale: Sirach forbids attempting a bribe because God will not accept it; Deuteronomy likewise explicitly denies that He takes bribes.
source_text: Do not bribe, for He will not accept it, and do not rely on an unjust sacrifice.

target_units.text: For the Lord your God, He is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great and mighty and fearful God, who shows no partiality, neither takes a bribe;

relationship: close impartial divine judgment
rationale: Sirach calls the Lord a judge without regard to prestige; Deuteronomy likewise denies divine partiality and names His judgment for vulnerable people.
source_text: For the Lord is judge, and with Him there is no prestige of persons.

target_units.text: For the Lord your God, He is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great and mighty and fearful God, who shows no partiality, neither takes a bribe;
who executes judgment for the sojourner, and the orphan, and the widow, and loves the sojourner, to give him bread and clothing.

relationship: parallel divine regard for the poor
rationale: Sirach promises an impartial hearing for the poor and wronged; the psalm likewise denies that the poor or the needy person's endurance will be forgotten.
source_text: He will not show partiality against the poor, and He will hear the petition of the wronged.

target_units.text: For the poor will not be forgotten utterly; the endurance of the needy will not perish for ever.

relationship: close divine hearing of widows and orphans
rationale: Both explicitly identify widows and orphans whose cries God hears, with Exodus warning those who afflict them.
source_text: He will certainly not disregard an orphan’s supplication or a widow when she pours out her words.

target_units.text: You shall not mistreat any widow or orphan.
But if you afflict them, and they cry aloud to Me, I will surely listen to their voice,
I will be angry with wrath and kill you with the sword. Your wives will become widows and your children orphans.

relationship: close widow's cry against her afflicter
rationale: Sirach makes the widow's cry rise against the cause of her tears; Exodus likewise joins afflicted widows' cries with God's response against the afflicters.
source_text: Do not a widow’s tears run down her cheek, and her cry rise against the one who brought them down?

target_units.text: You shall not mistreat any widow or orphan.
But if you afflict them, and they cry aloud to Me, I will surely listen to their voice,
I will be angry with wrath and kill you with the sword. Your wives will become widows and your children orphans.

relationship: parallel hearing of righteous supplication
rationale: Sirach says the acceptable servant's petition reaches the clouds; the psalm likewise places God's ears toward righteous supplication, without the cloud image.
source_text: The one who serves acceptably will be received, and his petition will reach as far as the clouds.

target_units.text: The Lord’s eyes are upon the righteous, and His ears toward their supplication.
But the Lord’s face is against those who do evil, to destroy their remembrance from the earth.
The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them; from all their afflictions He rescued them.

relationship: related acceptance of humble prayer
rationale: Sirach describes the humble person's prayer drawing near to God; Jesus presents the humbled tax collector's plea as accepted, without using the cloud image.
source_text: A humble person’s prayer has passed through the clouds, and until it draws near, he will certainly not be comforted.

target_units.text: But the tax collector, standing far away, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner.’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

relationship: close persistent petition until divine vindication
rationale: Sirach describes perseverance until God judges for the righteous; Jesus likewise urges persistent prayer and promises justice for those crying to God.
source_text: He will certainly not withdraw until the Most High visits, judges in favor of the righteous, and executes judgment.

target_units.text: And He told them a parable about their need to pray always and not lose heart,
saying, “There was a certain judge in a certain city who neither feared God nor respected any person.
And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him, saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’
For a time he was unwilling. But afterward he said within himself, ‘Even though I do not fear God or respect any person,
yet because this widow troubles me, I will give her justice, lest by coming continually she wear me down.’”
And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says.
And will not God bring about justice for His chosen ones who cry to Him day and night? And will He delay over them?
I tell you, He will bring about justice for them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?”

relationship: close assurance that divine justice will not delay
rationale: Both deny indefinite delay in God's response to the wronged petitioners; Luke explicitly promises speedy justice for His chosen ones.
source_text: The Lord will certainly not delay or be patient with them,

target_units.text: And will not God bring about justice for His chosen ones who cry to Him day and night? And will He delay over them?
I tell you, He will bring about justice for them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?”

relationship: parallel retribution against hostile powers
rationale: Sirach anticipates punishment of the merciless and repayment of nations; Deuteronomy likewise promises repayment against enemies and vengeance for God's people's blood.
source_text: until He crushes the loins of the merciless and repays the nations with retribution,

target_units.text: For I will sharpen My sword as lightning, and My hand shall lay hold of judgment; and I will repay a penalty unto the enemies, and unto them that hate Me will I repay.
I will make My arrows drunk with blood, and My sword shall devour flesh, from the blood of the slain and of captives, from the head of the rulers of the enemies.

Rejoice, O heavens, together with Him, and let all the sons of God worship Him; rejoice, O nations, with His people, and let all the angels of God give Him strength; for He avenges the blood of His sons, and shall avenge and repay a penalty unto the enemies, and unto them that hate Him shall He repay; and the Lord shall thoroughly cleanse the land of His people.

relationship: related breaking of oppressive rulers' power
rationale: Sirach describes crushed unjust scepters; Isaiah describes God shattering rulers' yoke in the lament over Babylon's king. The instruments of domination differ.
source_text: until He removes the multitude of the insolent and crushes the scepters of the unjust,

target_units.text: and you will take up this lament against Babylon’s king and say on that day, “How the one who made demands has rested, and the taskmaster rested!
God shattered the sinners’ yoke, the rulers’ yoke;
having struck a nation in wrath with an incurable blow, striking a nation with a blow of anger that did not spare,

relationship: close repayment according to deeds
rationale: Both explicitly describe God repaying each person according to actions, within an account of divine judgment.
source_text: until He repays a person according to his actions and judges human works according to their thoughts,

target_units.text: But by your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment,
who will repay each according to his works:
to those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruptibility, eternal life;
but to those acting from selfish ambition, who disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, wrath and fury,

relationship: close judgment of inward disposition and conduct
rationale: Sirach includes thoughts in the judgment of works; Jeremiah likewise joins examination of hearts with repayment according to ways and practices.
source_text: until He repays a person according to his actions and judges human works according to their thoughts,

target_units.text: The heart is deep beyond all things, and so is a human; and who will know him?
I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

relationship: close vindication and compassion for God's people
rationale: Sirach joins judgment of His people's case with mercy; Deuteronomy likewise says the Lord judges His people and is moved concerning His weakened servants.
source_text: until He judges His people’s case and gladdens them with His mercy.

target_units.text: For the Lord shall judge His people, and be moved concerning His servants; for He saw them weakened, and failing under assault, and exhausted.

relationship: related rain image for restoring divine aid
rationale: Sirach compares timely mercy during affliction with rain in drought; Hosea describes the healing Lord's coming as seasonal rain, within an appeal to return to Him.
source_text: Mercy is timely in the season of His people’s affliction, like rain clouds in a season without rain.

target_units.text: “Let us go and return to the Lord our God, because He has seized us and will heal us; He will strike and dress our wounds.
He will restore us to health after two days; on the third day we will rise and live before Him.
We will know; we will pursue knowledge of the Lord. We will find Him ready like dawn, and He will come to us like rain, early and late upon the land.”

relationship: parallel mercy leading to worldwide recognition
rationale: Sirach petitions for mercy and divine fear among nations; the psalm likewise petitions for compassion and blessing so God's way and salvation become known among nations.
source_text: Have mercy on us, Master, God of all; look upon us and cast Thy fear upon all the nations.

target_units.text: May God have compassion on us and bless us; may He make His face shine upon us. Diapsalma.
That Thy way may be known on earth, Thy salvation among all nations.

relationship: parallel visible divine power before nations
rationale: Sirach asks God to raise His hand so nations see His dominion; the psalm asks that vengeance be known among nations and invokes His great arm for rescue.
source_text: Raise Thy hand against foreign nations, and let them see Thy dominion.

target_units.text: lest the nations say, “Where is their God?” And let vengeance for the poured-out blood of Thy servants be known among the nations before our eyes.
Let the groaning of those in bonds enter before Thee; according to the greatness of Thine arm, preserve the sons of those put to death.

relationship: related divine sanctification before nations
rationale: Sirach links God's sanctification among His people with His magnification among nations; Ezekiel likewise connects sanctification in Israel before nations with recognition of the Lord.
source_text: Just as Thou wast sanctified in us before them, so mayest Thou be magnified in them before us.

target_units.text: I will sanctify My great name, profaned among the nations, which you profaned among them. The nations will know that I am the Lord when I am sanctified in you before their eyes.

relationship: close nations acknowledging the only God
rationale: Sirach asks nations to know that no God exists except the Lord; the psalm likewise joins all nations' worship with the affirmation that He alone is the great God.
source_text: Let them know Thee, as we also have known that there is no God except Thee, Lord.

target_units.text: There is none like Thee among gods, Lord, and nothing is like Thy works.
All the nations Thou madest will come and bow down before Thee, Lord, and glorify Thy name,
for Thou art great and dost wondrous things; Thou alone art the great God.

relationship: related divine wonders manifested before nations
rationale: Sirach asks for renewed signs and different wonders; Micah promises wonders like those of departure from Egypt, with nations seeing and fearing God.
source_text: Renew signs and make wonders different; glorify Thy hand and right arm.

target_units.text: And as in the days of your departure from Egypt, you will see wonderful things.
Nations will see and be ashamed of all their strength. They will place hands over their mouth; their ears will be deafened.
They will lick dust like snakes dragging along the earth; they will be thrown into turmoil in their confinement. They will be astonished at the Lord our God and fear Thee.

relationship: close petition for wrath against hostile nations
rationale: Both petition God to pour out wrath upon hostile nations; the psalm specifies their devastation of Jacob as the cause.
source_text: Rouse anger and pour out wrath; remove the adversary and destroy the enemy.

target_units.text: Pour out Thy wrath upon nations that do not know Thee, and upon kingdoms that did not call on Thy name,
for they devoured Jacob and made his place desolate.

relationship: related remembered oath and deliverance from enemies
rationale: Sirach asks God to remember the oath within a plea for deliverance; Zechariah likewise joins rescue from enemies with remembrance of the covenant and oath to Abraham.
source_text: Hasten the time and remember the oath, and let them recount Thy mighty deeds.

target_units.text: salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us,
to show mercy to our fathers and remember His holy covenant,
the oath He swore to Abraham our father, to grant us
that, rescued from our enemies’ hand, we might serve Him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before Him all our days.

relationship: close fiery wrath consuming enemies
rationale: Sirach asks for fiery destruction of those harming God's people; the psalm likewise describes enemies consumed by fire in the Lord's anger.
source_text: Let the survivor be consumed in fiery wrath, and let those who harm Thy people find destruction.

target_units.text: May your hand be found by all your enemies; may your right hand find all who hate you.
You will make them like a fiery furnace at the time of your presence; the Lord in His anger will throw them into turmoil, and fire will devour them.
You will destroy their fruit from the earth and their seed from the sons of men,

relationship: close crushing of enemies' heads
rationale: Both describe God crushing enemy heads; Sirach specifically identifies rulers asserting their own exclusiveness.
source_text: Crush the heads of enemy rulers who say, “There is no one except us.”

target_units.text: Nevertheless God will crush His enemies’ heads, the crown of hair of those walking in their offenses.

relationship: close gathering Israel and restoring inherited land
rationale: Sirach asks for Jacob's tribes to be gathered into their inheritance; Deuteronomy promises gathering the dispersed and bringing them into their fathers' land.
source_text: Gather all the tribes of Jacob, and give them their inheritance as from the beginning.

target_units.text: then the Lord shall heal your sins, and have mercy upon you, and shall gather you again from all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you.
If your dispersion is from one end of heaven unto the other end of heaven, from thence shall the Lord your God gather you, and from thence shall the Lord your God take you.
And the Lord your God shall bring you into the land which your fathers inherited, and you shall inherit it; and He shall do you good, and make you more numerous than your fathers.

relationship: close Israel designated God's firstborn
rationale: Sirach appeals to God's designation of Israel as firstborn; Exodus records that exact designation in the demand for Israel's release.
source_text: Have mercy, Lord, on the people called by Thy name, and on Israel, whom Thou didst liken to a firstborn.

target_units.text: And you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is My firstborn son.
And I said to you, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” If therefore you will not let them go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.’”

relationship: close appeal for the people bearing God's name
rationale: Both petitions appeal to God's mercy because His name has been called over His people; Daniel also explicitly names Israel and Zion.
source_text: Have mercy, Lord, on the people called by Thy name, and on Israel, whom Thou didst liken to a firstborn.

target_units.text: Attend with Thine ear, Lord, and hear me. Open Thine eyes and see our desolation and that of Thy city, over which Thy name has been called. For we make our supplication in our prayers before Thee because of Thy mercy, not our righteous deeds.
Lord, be propitious! Lord, hear and act, and do not delay, for Thine own sake, Master, because Thy name has been called over Thy city Zion and Thy people Israel.”

relationship: close Zion as God's chosen rest
rationale: Sirach calls Jerusalem God's sanctuary and resting place; the psalm likewise identifies chosen Zion as His enduring dwelling and rest.
source_text: Have compassion on the city of Thy sanctuary, Jerusalem, the place of Thy rest.

target_units.text: For the Lord chose Zion; He selected her as His dwelling:
“This is My rest for age upon age; here I will dwell, for I selected her.

relationship: parallel divine glory upon Jerusalem
rationale: Sirach asks for Zion to be filled with recounting God's excellence and the people with His glory; Isaiah announces the Lord's glory appearing over Jerusalem and attracting nations.
source_text: Fill Zion with the recounting of Thine excellence, and Thy people with Thy glory.

target_units.text: Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the Lord’s glory has risen upon you.
Behold, darkness and gloom will cover earth over nations, but the Lord will appear upon you, and His glory will be seen over you.
Kings will walk by your light, and nations by your radiance.

relationship: parallel establishment of prophetic words
rationale: Sirach asks God to uphold prophecies spoken in His name; Isaiah describes Him establishing His servant's words and making His messengers' counsel true.
source_text: Give testimony to those Thou didst create in the beginning, and raise up the prophecies spoken in Thy name.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord who redeems you and forms you from the womb: “I am the Lord who completes all things. I stretched heaven alone and established the earth. Who else
will scatter the signs of spirit-mediums and divinations from the heart, turning the discerning backward and making their counsel foolish,

and establish His servant’s words and make His messengers’ counsel true? He says to Jerusalem, ‘You will be inhabited,’ and to Judea’s cities, ‘You will be rebuilt,’ and her deserted places will spring up;

relationship: parallel divine goodness toward those who wait
rationale: Sirach petitions for a reward to those awaiting God; Lamentations likewise calls Him good to those waiting for Him and enduring for His salvation.
source_text: Give a reward to those who wait for Thee, and let Thy prophets be found trustworthy.

target_units.text: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul that will seek Him as good
and will endure and be quiet for the Lord’s salvation.

relationship: related confirmation of a prophet's faithfulness
rationale: Sirach asks that God's prophets be found trustworthy; Jeremiah describes fulfillment of a peace prophecy as the means of recognizing a prophet sent in faithfulness by the Lord.
source_text: Give a reward to those who wait for Thee, and let Thy prophets be found trustworthy.

target_units.text: The prophet who prophesied peace—when the word comes, they will know the prophet whom the Lord sent to them in faithfulness.

relationship: explicit reference to Aaron's blessing
rationale: Sirach appeals to Aaron's blessing concerning the people; Numbers records God's instruction to Aaron and his sons and the blessing they are to pronounce.
source_text: Hear, Lord, the petition of Thy supplicants, according to Aaron’s blessing concerning Thy people,

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying:
Speak unto Aaron and unto his sons, saying: Thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, saying unto them (and they shall put My name upon the sons of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them):
The Lord bless you and keep you;
the Lord make His face shine upon you, and have mercy upon you;
the Lord lift up His face upon you, and give you peace.

relationship: parallel blessing resulting in worldwide divine recognition
rationale: Sirach expects all earth to know the Lord after the petition and blessing; the psalm similarly joins blessing with salvation known among nations and fear at earth's ends.
source_text: and all those upon the earth will know that Thou art Lord, the God of the ages.

target_units.text: That Thy way may be known on earth, Thy salvation among all nations.
Let peoples give thanks unto Thee, God; let all peoples give thanks unto Thee.
Let nations rejoice and exult, for Thou wilt judge peoples in uprightness and guide nations upon the earth. Diapsalma.
Let peoples give thanks unto Thee, God; let all peoples give thanks unto Thee.
The earth gave its fruit; may God, our God, bless us.
May God bless us, and let all earth’s ends fear Him.

relationship: related food-and-stomach formulation with differing conclusions
rationale: Both join food and the stomach; Sirach distinguishes better foods, while Paul emphasizes their transience and the body's belonging to the Lord.
source_text: The belly will eat every food, yet one food is better than another.

target_units.text: Foods are for the stomach, and the stomach for foods, but God will bring both it and them to an end. Yet the body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

relationship: close tasting food as an analogy for discerning words
rationale: Both compare bodily tasting with discernment of speech; Sirach names the understanding heart and false words, while Job names the discerning ear.
source_text: The throat tastes food from the hunt; so an understanding heart tastes false words.

target_units.text: For the ear discerns words, and the throat tastes food.

relationship: related comparison distinguishing one daughter from others
rationale: Sirach says one daughter is better than another; the husband's praise in Proverbs similarly distinguishes one woman above many accomplished daughters. Sirach's opening clause has no counterpart there.
source_text: A woman will accept any male, yet one daughter is better than another.

target_units.text: “Many daughters acquired wealth, many did mighty things, but you stand above and have surpassed them all.”

relationship: related delight in one's wife
rationale: Sirach describes a woman's beauty gladdening the face; Proverbs likewise commends joy with one's wife and delight in her affection, without ranking beauty above every desire.
source_text: A woman’s beauty gladdens the face and surpasses every human desire.

target_units.text: Let your fountain of water be your own, and share joy with the wife of your youth.

Let a deer of affection and a colt of your graces keep company with you. Let your own woman lead you and be with you at every time, for as you move in the company of her affection, you will be one among many.

relationship: contrast in the assessment of beauty
rationale: Sirach celebrates beauty's power to gladden and attract; Proverbs calls beauty vain while praising understanding and fear of the Lord. Their emphases are distinct.
source_text: A woman’s beauty gladdens the face and surpasses every human desire.

target_units.text: A woman’s pleasing qualities are false and beauty is vain; for an understanding woman is blessed, and let her praise the fear of the Lord.

relationship: related merciful speech and a wife's benefit to her family
rationale: Sirach joins mercy and gentleness on a wife's tongue with her husband's distinction; Proverbs likewise joins wise speech and mercy with flourishing children and the husband's praise.
source_text: If mercy and gentleness are upon her tongue, her husband is unlike ordinary human sons.

target_units.text: She opens her mouth wisely and according to law, and her mercy raised up her children, and they became wealthy, and her husband praised her:

relationship: close wife as a corresponding helper
rationale: Sirach calls the acquired wife a helper corresponding to the husband; Genesis explicitly describes the making of that corresponding helper and the resulting marital union.
source_text: The one who acquires a wife begins a possession: a helper corresponding to him and a pillar of rest.

target_units.text: And the Lord God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. Let Us make him a helper corresponding to him.”

And God also formed from the earth every wild beast of the field and every bird of heaven, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. And whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.
And Adam gave names to all the cattle, all the birds of heaven, and all the wild beasts of the field. But for Adam no helper like himself was found.
And God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept. And He took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh.
And the Lord God fashioned the rib He had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam.
And Adam said: This, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called Woman, for she was taken from her husband.
For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.

relationship: close nest imagery for the displaced person
rationale: Sirach describes the unsettled person as having no nest; Proverbs likewise compares estrangement from one's own place with a bird departing its nest, with a different stated consequence.
source_text: So it is with a person who has no nest and lodges wherever evening overtakes him.

target_units.text: As when a bird flies down from its own nest, so a person is enslaved when estranged from his own places.

relationship: parallel distinction between professed and dependable friendship
rationale: Sirach 37 contrasts friendship's name with its reality; the earlier passage likewise requires testing because some companions abandon their friend in affliction.
source_text: Every friend will say, “I too have shown friendship,” but there is a friend who is a friend in name alone.

target_units.text: If you acquire a friend, acquire him through testing, and do not trust him quickly.
For there is a friend for his own occasion who will certainly not remain on the day of your affliction.
There is also a friend who turns to enmity and will expose a quarrel to your reproach.
There is also a friend who shares your tables but will certainly not remain on the day of your affliction.

relationship: close pain caused by a companion's enmity
rationale: Sirach describes a friend's change to enmity as grievous; the psalm likewise distinguishes the painful betrayal of a close companion from an ordinary enemy's reproach.
source_text: Is there not grief to the point of death when a companion and friend turns to enmity?

target_units.text: For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have endured it; and if the one hating me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him.
But you, a man of like soul, my leader and my acquaintance,
you who made food sweet together with me: in God’s house we walked in concord.

relationship: close friend sharing prosperity but opposing the afflicted
rationale: Both describe a companion enjoying shared prosperity or meals who becomes hostile when the friend is brought low.
source_text: A companion enjoys his friend’s gladness but will stand against him in a time of affliction.

target_units.text: There is also a friend who shares your tables but will certainly not remain on the day of your affliction.
In your prosperity he will be like you, and he will speak freely to your household slaves;
if you are brought low, he will be against you and hide from your face.

relationship: parallel refusal to abandon an established friend
rationale: Sirach warns against forgetting a friend in wealth; Proverbs likewise forbids abandoning one's friend, without limiting the warning to prosperity.
source_text: Do not forget a friend in your soul or be unmindful of him in your wealth.

target_units.text: Do not abandon your friend or an ancestral friend, and do not enter your brother’s house when misfortune strikes you; a nearby friend is better than a brother dwelling far away.

relationship: narrative example of self-interested counsel
rationale: Sirach warns that some counselors advise for themselves; Absalom's favorable assurances and proposal that he become judge win the people's hearts for himself.
source_text: Every counselor exalts counsel, but there is someone who counsels for himself.

target_units.text: Absalom would rise early and stand beside the road to the gate. Whenever a man with a case came before the king for judgment, Absalom called to him, “What city are you from?” The man would answer, “Your servant is from one of Israel’s tribes.”
Absalom would say to him, “Your claims are good and straightforward, but no one from the king is here to hear you.”
Absalom would say, “Who will appoint me judge in the land, so that every man with a dispute or case will come to me and I will give him justice?”
Whenever a man approached to bow down to him, Absalom would stretch out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him warmly.
Absalom did this to all Israel who came to the king for judgment. Absalom made the hearts of the men of Israel his own.

relationship: related favorable speech concealing hostile intent
rationale: Sirach's counselor praises a road but stands opposite to watch the outcome; Proverbs likewise describes an enemy agreeing with his lips while devising deceit within.
source_text: and say to you, “Your road is good,” then stand opposite to see what happens to you.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;

relationship: related caution about an apparently friendly enemy
rationale: Sirach warns against confiding counsel to suspicious or envious people; Proverbs likewise warns against persuasion by an enemy's appealing speech and concealed hostility.
source_text: Do not take counsel with someone who looks suspiciously at you, and hide your counsel from those who envy you.

target_units.text: A weeping enemy agrees to everything with his lips, but in his heart devises deceits;
if the enemy entreats you with a loud voice, do not be persuaded, for seven evils are in his life.
One who hides enmity establishes deceit, but one well known in councils discloses his own sins.

relationship: close godliness and dependable friendship
rationale: Sirach 37 commends the godly companion who shares pain; Sirach 6 likewise links faithful, life-supporting friendship with fear of the Lord.
source_text: Instead, remain with a godly man whom you know to keep commandments, whose soul is in accord with your soul, and who will share your pain if you stumble.

target_units.text: A faithful friend is a strong shelter; and whoever has found him has found a treasure.
There is no exchange for a faithful friend, and no weight to measure his excellence.
A faithful friend is medicine for life, and those who fear the Lord will find him.
The one who fears the Lord will guide his friendship rightly, for as he is, so also is his neighbor.

relationship: contrast between inward counsel and rash confidence
rationale: Sirach commends one's heart's counsel amid advice about godly companionship and prayer; Proverbs specifically condemns trusting a rash heart and commends walking in wisdom. Rashness is not attributed to every inward judgment.
source_text: Establish the counsel of your heart, for you have nothing more trustworthy than it.

target_units.text: One who trusts in a rash heart is a fool; but one who walks in wisdom will be saved.

relationship: close prayer for a rightly directed path
rationale: Sirach commands petitioning God to straighten one's road in truth; the psalm similarly asks Him to show the way and lead the speaker on level ground.
source_text: Besides all these things, petition the Most High to make your road straight in truth.

target_units.text: Make Thy mercy heard by me in the morning, for I hoped in Thee. Make known to me, Lord, the way I shall walk, for unto Thee I lifted my soul.
Take me out from my enemies, Lord, for I fled unto Thee for refuge.
Teach me to do Thy will, for Thou art my God. Thy good Spirit will lead me on level ground.

relationship: close counsel preceding action
rationale: Sirach says counsel precedes every action; Proverbs likewise directly instructs the hearer to do everything with counsel. Sirach also names the initiating word.
source_text: A word is the beginning of every work, and counsel precedes every action.

target_units.text: Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel. The powerful are hot-tempered, but let them not drink wine,

relationship: related fourfold moral alternatives explained by context
rationale: Sirach's four parts are named in 37:18 as good, evil, life and death; Deuteronomy presents those same four alternatives and connects a turning heart with their outcome.
source_text: The trace of a heart’s change brings forth four parts:

target_units.text: Behold, I have set before your face this day life and death, good and evil.

If you obey the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you this day, to love the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His ordinances and His judgments, then you shall live and be many; and the Lord your God shall bless you in all the land into which you go to inherit it.
And if your heart turns aside, and you will not hearken, and you are led astray to bow down unto other gods and serve them,
I declare unto you this day that you shall surely perish, and you shall in no wise be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you, into which you are crossing the Jordan to inherit it.
I call heaven and earth to witness unto you this day: I have set before your face life and death, the blessing and the curse. Choose life, that you and your seed may live,

relationship: close life and death under the tongue's power
rationale: Sirach says the tongue rules good, evil, life and death; Proverbs likewise places life and death in the tongue's hand, using a closely related agency image.
source_text: good and evil, life and death; the tongue continually rules them.

target_units.text: Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who control it will eat its fruits.

relationship: close teacher failing to benefit himself
rationale: Sirach describes a capable instructor useless to his own soul; Paul likewise questions the teacher who instructs others while failing to teach himself and transgressing his instruction.
source_text: There is a skillful man who instructs many, yet is useless to his own soul.

target_units.text: and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness,
an instructor of the senseless, a teacher of infants, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you then who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?
You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
You who boast in law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law?

relationship: contrast in socially rejected wisdom
rationale: Sirach describes a speaker displaying wisdom yet hated and lacking food; the next verse denies him wisdom. Ecclesiastes instead affirms the genuine wisdom of the poor man whose wisdom is despised and whose words are unheard.
source_text: There is someone who displays wisdom in words but is hated; this person will lack all food,

target_units.text: and he might find in it a poor wise man, who will deliver the city by his wisdom; yet no one remembered that poor man.
I said, Wisdom is better than strength; yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.
The words of the wise, heard quietly, are better than the shouting of rulers in follies.

relationship: related understanding's fruit upon the mouth
rationale: Sirach links personal wisdom with trustworthy fruits of understanding upon the mouth; Proverbs likewise describes good filling a person's life from the mouth's fruits.
source_text: There is someone wise for his own soul, and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy upon his mouth.

target_units.text: From fruits of a mouth a man’s life will be filled with good things, and the recompense of his lips will be given to him.

relationship: parallel wise teacher instructing the people
rationale: Sirach says the wise man instructs his people; Ecclesiastes is likewise described as wise and teaching the people knowledge. Sirach additionally calls the fruits trustworthy.
source_text: A wise man will instruct his own people, and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy.

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.

relationship: close blessedness associated with wisdom
rationale: Sirach calls the wise man blessed and recognized as happy; Proverbs likewise calls the person who finds wisdom blessed, without the observers' testimony.
source_text: A wise man will be filled with blessing, and all who see him will call him happy.

target_units.text: Blessed is the person who found wisdom, the mortal who saw good sense,

relationship: related contrast between mortal duration and enduring Israel
rationale: Sirach contrasts numbered human days with Israel's unnumbered days; Jeremiah grounds Israel's continuing nationhood in the enduring celestial order, rather than an individual's lifespan.
source_text: A man’s life is a number of days, but Israel’s days are beyond numbering.

target_units.text: Thus said the Lord, who gave the sun for daylight, moon and stars for night light, and a cry in the sea so its waves boomed—the Lord Almighty is His name:
If these laws cease from before Me, says the Lord, then Israel’s family will cease to be a nation before Me for all days.

relationship: parallel enduring remembrance of the virtuous
rationale: Sirach promises the wise person's name enduring life among the people; the psalm similarly promises the righteous person an everlasting memorial.
source_text: The wise person will inherit trust among his people, and his name will live for ever.

target_units.text: For he will never be shaken; the righteous person will be an everlasting memorial.

relationship: parallel refusing desires harmful to the soul
rationale: Sirach 37 requires examining what harms one's soul and withholding it; Sirach 18 likewise commands restraint of appetites and warns against supplying every desire.
source_text: Child, in your life test your soul; see what is bad for it and do not give it that.

target_units.text: Do not walk after your desires, and restrain your appetites.
If you supply your soul with the satisfaction of desire, it will make you an object of your enemies’ gloating.

relationship: related limits of what is beneficial
rationale: Sirach denies that everything benefits everyone; Paul likewise distinguishes what is permitted from what benefits or builds up. Sirach also notes differing individual pleasures.
source_text: For not everything benefits everyone, and not every soul takes pleasure in everything.

target_units.text: All things are permitted, but not all things are beneficial. All things are permitted, but not all things build up.

relationship: close warning against insatiable desire for food
rationale: Sirach forbids abandoning oneself to luxurious dishes; Proverbs likewise warns the insatiable diner not to desire the ruler's foods.
source_text: Do not be insatiable in every luxury, and do not abandon yourself to dishes of food.

target_units.text: If you sit to dine at the table of rulers, thoughtfully consider what is set before you,
and lay your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things;
but if you are more insatiable, do not desire his foods, for these belong to a false life.

relationship: close overeating followed by vomiting
rationale: Sirach links excessive food with illness and vomiting; Proverbs gives honey as the specific example, warning that fullness leads to vomiting.
source_text: For with much food there will be illness, and insatiability will approach the point of bilious vomiting.

target_units.text: Having found honey, eat what is sufficient, lest you become full and vomit.

relationship: parallel bodily benefit of restrained eating
rationale: Sirach 37 contrasts deadly insatiability with life-preserving care; Sirach 31 similarly contrasts a moderate stomach's healthy sleep with the insatiable person's physical distress.
source_text: Many have died through insatiability, but the one who takes care will add life.

target_units.text: How sufficient a little is for an instructed person! He does not pant upon his bed.
Healthy sleep comes with a moderate stomach. He rose early, and his soul was with him. The pain of sleeplessness, bilious vomiting, and cramp accompany an insatiable man.

relationship: related honorable recognition of a physician
rationale: Sirach commands honoring the physician; Paul's greeting expressly calls Luke the beloved physician. The greeting positively identifies a physician without repeating the creation claim.
source_text: Honor a physician with his due honors, according to the need for him; for the Lord created him also.

target_units.text: Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and Demas.

relationship: close attribution of healing to God
rationale: Sirach says healing comes from the Most High; Exodus explicitly identifies the Lord as the people's healer. The physician's royal gift is additional in Sirach.
source_text: For healing is from the Most High, and the physician will receive a gift from a king.

target_units.text: and said, “If you diligently listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is pleasing before Him, and give ear to His commandments, and keep all His ordinances, I will bring upon you none of the diseases which I brought upon the Egyptians; for I am the Lord who heals you.”

relationship: related professional skill recognized before rulers
rationale: Sirach says medical knowledge brings honor before dignitaries; Proverbs likewise places the perceptive worker beside kings, without specifying medicine.
source_text: A physician’s knowledge will raise his head, and he will be admired before dignitaries.

target_units.text: A perceptive man, keen in his works, must stand beside kings and not stand beside sluggish men.

relationship: narrative example of a natural remedy within divine healing
rationale: Sirach commends medicines made from earth; Hezekiah's promised divine healing includes applying a cake of figs to his ulcer. The narrative gives one concrete remedy, not a general pharmacology.
source_text: The Lord created medicines from the earth, and a prudent man will not reject them.

target_units.text: ‘Return and tell Hezekiah, leader of My people: Thus says the Lord, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Behold, I shall heal you; on the third day you shall go up to the Lord’s house,
and I shall add fifteen years to your days. I shall save you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and shield this city for My own sake and for the sake of David My servant.’
He said, ‘Let them take a cake of figs and place it on the ulcer, and he will recover.’

relationship: direct narrative counterpart of wood sweetening water
rationale: Sirach recalls water sweetened by wood; Exodus narrates Moses casting the divinely shown wood into Marah's bitter water and its becoming sweet.
source_text: Was not water sweetened by wood, so that its strength might be known?

target_units.text: They came to Marah but could not drink its water because it was bitter. Therefore that place was named Bitterness.
The people murmured against Moses, saying, “What shall we drink?”

And Moses cried to the Lord; and the Lord showed him a piece of wood, and he cast it into the water, and the water was made sweet. There He appointed ordinances and judgments for him, and there He tested him,

relationship: parallel God-given knowledge for skilled works
rationale: Sirach attributes human knowledge to God in the context of useful works; Exodus expressly attributes Bezalel's knowledge and craftsmanship to divine empowerment, in sanctuary construction.
source_text: He Himself gave human beings knowledge, to be glorified in His wonderful works.

target_units.text: The Lord spoke to Moses, saying,
“Behold, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
I have filled him with a divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of work,
to plan and design, to work in gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, spun scarlet yarn, and spun fine linen,
to work in stone and the woodworking crafts, and to perform every kind of work.

relationship: close perfumer's preparation of a compound
rationale: Sirach mentions the perfumer making a mixture; Exodus explicitly describes a compound prepared by a perfumer's skill. Exodus's purpose is holy anointing oil, not the medicinal relief preceding Sirach's clause.
source_text: By these He healed and removed the sufferer’s pain; with these a perfumer will make a mixture,

target_units.text: The Lord spoke to Moses, saying,
“Take spices: five hundred shekels of the choicest myrrh, half as much fragrant cinnamon, two hundred and fifty, and two hundred and fifty of fragrant cane,
five hundred sanctuary shekels of iris, and a hin of olive oil.
Make these into holy anointing oil, a compound prepared by a perfumer’s skill. It shall be holy anointing oil.

relationship: close prayer for divine healing during illness
rationale: Sirach instructs the sick person to pray to the Lord for healing; James likewise prescribes prayer during sickness and attributes the person's restoration to the Lord.
source_text: Child, do not be negligent in your illness, but pray to the Lord, and He Himself will heal you.

target_units.text: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the Lord’s name.
And the prayer of faith will save the weary sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. A righteous person’s petition has great strength when it is at work.

relationship: close repentance involving hands and heart
rationale: Sirach joins putting away wrongdoing with straightened hands and a cleansed heart; James likewise calls sinners to cleanse hands and purify hearts.
source_text: Put wrongdoing away, straighten your hands, and cleanse your heart from every sin.

target_units.text: Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you of divided mind.

relationship: close fine-flour memorial and fragrant offering
rationale: Sirach commands a fragrant offering and memorial of fine flour; Leviticus prescribes fine flour, frankincense and a memorial portion offered as a sweet savor.
source_text: Give a fragrant offering and a memorial of fine flour, and make your offering rich, as one who is no more.

target_units.text: And if a soul brings a gift as a sacrifice unto the Lord, his gift shall be fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense upon it. It is a sacrifice.

And he shall bring it unto the sons of Aaron, the priests; and when he has taken from it a full handful of the fine flour with the oil and all its frankincense, the priest shall place its memorial portion upon the altar: a sacrifice, a sweet savour unto the Lord.
And what remains of the sacrifice shall be Aaron’s and his sons’; it is most holy among the sacrifices of the Lord.

relationship: close recognition that sick people need a physician
rationale: Sirach insists that the physician remain because the patient needs him; Jesus likewise states sick people's need for a physician, using that fact to explain His call to sinners.
source_text: Give the physician a place too, for the Lord created him; do not let him leave you, for you need him.

target_units.text: Jesus answered them, “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

relationship: related human petition for God to grant healing
rationale: Sirach describes physicians asking God for successful life-preserving healing; the believers in Acts likewise petition God to extend His hand for healing. Their roles and means differ.
source_text: for they themselves will petition the Lord to grant them success in relief and healing for the sake of preserving life.

target_units.text: And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant Thy servants to speak Thy word with all boldness,
while Thou stretchest out Thy hand for healing, and signs and wonders take place through the name of Thy holy Servant Jesus.”

relationship: narrative example of mourning joined with burial care
rationale: Sirach requires lament and due burial for the dead; Abraham likewise mourns Sarah and then seeks a burial possession for her.
source_text: Child, shed tears over the dead and begin a lament as one suffering terribly. Lay out his body according to his due, and do not neglect his burial.

target_units.text: And Sarah died in the city of Arbok, which is in the hollow, that is, Hebron, in the land of Canaan; and Abraham came to lament Sarah and to mourn.
And Abraham rose up from his dead, and spoke to the sons of Heth, saying,
“I am a resident foreigner and a sojourner among you. So give me a possession for burial among you, that I may bury my dead away from me.”

relationship: related fervent mourning with a stated duration
rationale: Sirach prescribes fervent lament for one or two days; Joseph's mourning for his father is likewise intense and bounded, but lasts seven days and has a different stated setting.
source_text: Make your weeping bitter and your lament fervent; mourn according to his worth for one day or two because of slander, and be comforted because of grief.

target_units.text: And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan; and they lamented him with a great and exceedingly grievous lamentation, and he mourned his father seven days.

relationship: close bodily weakening through grief
