rationale: Sirach says grief bends strength and can bring death; Proverbs likewise says the sorrowful person's bones dry up, contrasting a rejoicing heart.
source_text: For death comes from grief, and grief of heart will bend strength.

target_units.text: A rejoicing heart makes one flourish, but a sorrowful man’s bones dry up.

relationship: close refusal to surrender the heart to grief
rationale: Both command refusing grief and putting it away; Sirach 30 further commands comforting the heart and warns that grief destroys and brings no benefit.
source_text: Do not give your heart over to grief; put it away, remembering the last things.

target_units.text: Do not give your soul over to grief, and do not afflict yourself with your deliberation.
Gladness of heart is a person’s life, and a man’s rejoicing is length of days.
Beguile your soul, comfort your heart, and put grief far from you; for grief has destroyed many, and there is no benefit in it.

relationship: close stopping futile mourning because the dead do not return
rationale: Sirach says continued grief cannot benefit the dead; David similarly asks why he should continue fasting when he cannot bring his dead child back.
source_text: Do not forget: there is no return. You will not benefit this person, and you will harm yourself.

target_units.text: David said, “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, because I said, ‘Who knows whether the Lord will have mercy on me and the child will live?’
But now he has died. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”

relationship: parallel shared mortal destiny
rationale: The dead person's warning in Sirach says the hearer faces the same judgment; Ecclesiastes likewise says one event reaches everyone and that people go to the dead.
source_text: “Remember my judgment, for yours is likewise: yesterday for me, today for you.”

target_units.text: There is futility in everything: one event comes to the righteous and the ungodly, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. As the good person, so the sinner; as the one who swears, so the one who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: one event comes to everyone. Moreover, the heart of human beings is full of evil, and delirium is in their heart during their lives; afterward they go to the dead.

relationship: narrative example of resuming life after bereavement
rationale: Sirach commands rest from mourning once the dead person rests; David rises, worships and eats after his child's death, explaining that the child cannot return.
source_text: When the dead person rests, bring his remembrance to rest, and be comforted concerning him when his spirit departs.

target_units.text: David understood that his servants were whispering and perceived that the child had died. David said to his servants, “Has the child died?” They said, “He has died.”

David rose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and changed his clothes. He entered God’s house and bowed down to Him. Then he entered his own house and asked for bread to eat; they set bread before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, “What is this that you have done? While the child was still alive, you fasted and wept and kept vigil, but when the child died, you rose and ate bread and drank.”
David said, “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, because I said, ‘Who knows whether the Lord will have mercy on me and the child will live?’
But now he has died. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”

relationship: related attention to the work of cultivation
rationale: Sirach describes the farmer's attention to furrows and fodder; Isaiah likewise attends to plowing and leveling land before sowing. Its sowing example does not repeat Sirach's fodder clause or judgment about scribal leisure.
source_text: He will give his heart to making furrows, and his wakefulness to fodder for heifers.

target_units.text: Will the plowman plow all day? Or will he prepare seed before working the ground?
When he has leveled its surface, does he not then sow a little black cumin and cumin, and again sow wheat, barley and emmer within your borders?

relationship: close skilled work of seal engraving
rationale: Sirach includes workers engraving signets among devoted craftsmen; Exodus specifies stoneworker's seal-engraving craftsmanship for the inscribed memorial stones, with a different design and sacred purpose.
source_text: So also every craftsman and master-builder who spends the night like the day, those who engrave signet engravings: his persistence is in varying the design. He will give his heart to making the depiction lifelike, and his wakefulness to finishing the work.

target_units.text: You shall take two emerald stones and engrave the names of the sons of Israel on them,
six names on one stone and the six remaining names on the other, according to their generations.
With a stoneworker’s craftsmanship, like a seal engraving, you shall engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel.

You shall place the two stones on the shoulders of the shoulder-piece. They are memorial stones for the sons of Israel, and Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on his two shoulders before the Lord as a memorial concerning them.

relationship: shared image of a smith working with fire
rationale: Sirach describes the smith laboring by furnace heat; Isaiah employs a smith blowing coals and producing an implement as a comparison in God's address. It does not identify Sirach's vessel with that implement.
source_text: So also a smith sitting near an anvil and studying works of iron: the fire’s vapor will melt his flesh, and he will struggle in the furnace’s heat. He will incline his ear to the hammer’s sound, and his eyes are upon the pattern of the vessel. He will give his heart to completing works, and his wakefulness to finishing their adornment.

target_units.text: Behold, I am creating you, not like a smith blowing coals and bringing out an implement for work. I did not create you for ruin, to destroy

relationship: related close observation of a working potter
rationale: Sirach describes a potter's anxious, continuous work at his wheel; Jeremiah observes a potter working upon stones and remaking a failed vessel. The details of the equipment remain distinct.
source_text: So also a potter sitting at his work and turning a wheel with his feet, who is continually anxious over his work, and whose whole labor is measured by number.

target_units.text: Rise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear My words.
And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was doing work upon the stones.
And the vessel he was making fell apart in his hands, and again he made it another vessel, as pleased him to make.

relationship: close labor of shaping clay for service
rationale: Sirach depicts the potter exerting his arm and finishing clay work; Wisdom likewise describes laborious kneading and shaping of vessels, before its separate warning about making idols.
source_text: With his arm he will shape clay, and before his feet he will bend his strength. He will give his heart to completing the coating, and his wakefulness to cleaning the kiln.

target_units.text: For a potter, laboriously kneading soft earth, shapes each object for our service; from the same clay he fashioned alike vessels serving clean purposes and those serving the opposite; and the clay-worker decides the use of each kind.

relationship: parallel recognition of skilled manual craftsmanship
rationale: Sirach recognizes each artisan's skill in his work; Exodus likewise enumerates skilled metal, stone, wood and textile work, explicitly attributing their abilities to God.
source_text: All these trusted in their hands, and each shows skill in his own work.

target_units.text: Moses said to the sons of Israel, “Behold, God has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
He has filled him with the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge of all things,
to design in every craft, working gold, silver, and bronze,
to work stone and shape wood, and to carry out every work of skill.
He has put it in his mind to teach—both him and Eliab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.

He has filled them with wisdom and understanding of mind to comprehend and do all the work of the sanctuary: weaving and embroidering in scarlet and fine linen, carrying out every work of design and embroidery.”

relationship: literary contrast between artisans and the learned person before rulers
rationale: Sirach denies the described artisans high standing in the assembly and a judge's seat; the following portrait instead places the learned person among dignitaries and rulers. This is the author's contrast of social roles.
source_text: Yet they will not be sought for the people’s council or rise high in the assembly; they will not sit on a judge’s chair or consider a covenant of judgment.

target_units.text: He will serve among dignitaries and appear before rulers. He will pass through the land of foreign nations, for he has experienced good and evil among human beings.

relationship: literary contrast between craft labor and study of instruction
rationale: Sirach distinguishes artisans sustaining the world from teachers of judgment and proverbs; the following portrait explicitly turns to study of law, ancient wisdom, prophecies and parables.
source_text: They will certainly not make instruction and judgment known or be found among proverbs, but they will sustain the fabric of the world, and their petition is in the work of their craft.

target_units.text: Different is the one who gives his soul to considering the law of the Most High: he will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients and occupy himself with prophecies.
He will preserve the discourse of renowned men and enter into the turns of parables.
He will seek out the hidden meanings of proverbs and dwell among the riddles of parables.

relationship: close sustained meditation on the Lord's law
rationale: Sirach describes a person devoted to considering God's law; the psalm likewise describes continual meditation upon that law. Sirach further names ancient wisdom and prophecies.
source_text: Different is the one who gives his soul to considering the law of the Most High: he will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients and occupy himself with prophecies.

target_units.text: but his will is in the Lord’s law, and on His law he will meditate day and night.

relationship: related preservation of inherited discourse through parables
rationale: Sirach joins preserving renowned discourse with entering parables; the psalm likewise joins parables and ancient riddles with what the fathers recounted and transmission to another generation.
source_text: He will preserve the discourse of renowned men and enter into the turns of parables.

target_units.text: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from the beginning,
whatever we heard and knew, and our fathers recounted to us,
it was not hidden from their children for another generation, as we announce the Lord’s praises, His mighty acts and the wonders He did.

relationship: close understanding of proverbs and riddles
rationale: Both portray growing wisdom through understanding obscure sayings, wise utterances and riddles, matching Sirach's search into parables' hidden meanings.
source_text: He will seek out the hidden meanings of proverbs and dwell among the riddles of parables.

target_units.text: For a wise person who hears these things will become wiser, and the discerning will acquire guidance,
and understand a comparison and an obscure saying, the utterances of the wise and riddles.

relationship: narrative example of learned people serving before a king
rationale: Sirach places the experienced learned man before rulers; Daniel and his companions receive knowledge and understanding, are examined by the king and remain beside him.
source_text: He will serve among dignitaries and appear before rulers. He will pass through the land of foreign nations, for he has experienced good and evil among human beings.

target_units.text: The Lord gave the young men knowledge, understanding, and practical wisdom in every literary skill; to Daniel He gave understanding in every utterance, vision, dreams, and all wisdom.
After these days the king ordered them brought in, and the chief eunuch brought them before King Nebuchadnezzar.
The king conversed with them, and among the wise no one was found like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. They remained beside the king.

In every matter of discourse, understanding, and education about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times wiser than the learned experts and philosophers throughout his kingdom. The king honored them, appointed them rulers, and declared them wiser than all his own men in affairs throughout his land and kingdom.

relationship: close morning petition before God
rationale: Sirach describes rising early to petition the Lord; the psalm likewise combines petition with standing before Him and being heard in the morning.
source_text: He will give his heart to rising early before the Lord his Maker and petition the Most High. He will open his mouth in prayer and petition concerning his sins.

target_units.text: Give ear to my words, Lord; understand my cry.
Attend to the voice of my petition, my King and my God, for unto Thee I will pray, Lord.
In the morning Thou wilt hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before Thee and watch.

relationship: related divinely granted wisdom expressed in words
rationale: Sirach describes understanding granted if the Lord wills and resulting words of wisdom; Paul likewise describes words of wisdom and knowledge distributed through the Spirit as He wills.
source_text: If the great Lord is willing, he will be filled with a spirit of understanding. He himself will rain down words of his wisdom and give thanks to the Lord in prayer.

target_units.text: For to one a word of wisdom is given through the Spirit, and to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit;
to another faith in the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit;
to another acts of power, to another prophecy, to another discernments of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, and to another interpretation of tongues.
But the one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually just as He wills.

relationship: related God-given understanding of hidden things
rationale: Sirach describes rightly directed knowledge considering God's hidden things; Daniel thanks God for wisdom and revelation of a mystery, expressly praising His disclosure of deep things.
source_text: He will direct his counsel and knowledge rightly and consider His hidden things.

target_units.text: Then, in a vision that very night, the king’s mystery was plainly revealed to Daniel. Daniel blessed the Lord Most High,
and cried out, “The name of the great Lord will be blessed for ever, because wisdom and majesty belong to Him.
He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,
reveals deep and dark things, knows what is in darkness and what is in light, and with Him is a dwelling.
To Thee, Lord of my fathers, I give thanks and praise, because Thou hast given me wisdom and prudence. Now Thou hast shown me everything I requested, to disclose these things to the king.”

relationship: parallel declaring divine instruction and delighting in it
rationale: Sirach's teacher reveals instruction and boasts in covenant law; the psalmist likewise declares God's judgments with his lips and delights in His testimonies.
source_text: He will reveal the instruction of his teaching and boast in the law of the Lord’s covenant.

target_units.text: Blessed art Thou, Lord; teach me Thine ordinances.
With my lips I declared all the judgments of Thy mouth.
In the way of Thy testimonies I delighted, as in all wealth.
I will ponder Thy commandments and consider Thy ways.
I will meditate on Thine ordinances; I will not forget Thy words.

relationship: close praised memory contrasted with an extinguished name
rationale: Sirach promises lasting praise, memory and name to the learned person; Proverbs likewise associates righteous memory with praise, contrasting the extinguished name of the impious.
source_text: Many will praise his understanding, and it will not be erased for ever. His memory will not depart, and his name will live for generations of generations.

target_units.text: The memory of righteous people is with praises, but the name of the impious is extinguished.

relationship: narrative example of foreign praise for wisdom
rationale: Sirach anticipates nations recounting wisdom; the queen of Sheba reports Solomon's fame in her land and praises his discernment and the God who appointed him.
source_text: Nations will recount his wisdom, and the assembly will proclaim his praise.

target_units.text: She said to King Solomon, “The report I heard in my land about your word and your discernment is true.
I did not believe those speaking to me until I arrived and my eyes saw. Behold, it is not half as they reported to me! You have added good things beyond them, beyond every report I heard in my land.
Blessed are your women! Blessed are these attendants of yours who stand before you continually, hearing all your discernment!

Blessed be the Lord your God, who delighted in you, setting you on Israel’s throne! Because the Lord loves Israel, to establish them for ever, He made you king over them to carry out judgment in righteousness and in their judgments.”

relationship: related high valuation of a name
rationale: Sirach values the learned person's leaving a name greater than a thousand; Proverbs likewise values a good name above much wealth. The comparisons differ, and Proverbs does not repeat Sirach's statement about resting.
source_text: If he remains, he will leave a name greater than a thousand; if he rests, it suffices for him.

target_units.text: A good name is more desirable than much wealth, and good favor is above silver and gold.

relationship: shared image of flourishing beside water
rationale: Sirach calls holy sons to sprout like a rose beside a stream; the psalm compares the law-meditating person with a fruitful tree beside waters. The plants differ.
source_text: Listen to me, holy sons, and sprout like a rose growing beside a flowing stream.

target_units.text: He will be like the tree planted beside the outlets of waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and whose leaf will not fall off; and everything he does will be prospered.

relationship: close lily blossom and fragrant growth imagery
rationale: Sirach calls the hearers to blossom like lilies and give fragrance; Hosea likewise describes restored Israel blossoming like a lily and spreading fragrance. Sirach directs this imagery toward praise.
source_text: Give a fragrant scent like frankincense, and blossom like a lily. Spread a scent and offer a song of praise; bless the Lord for all His works.

target_units.text: I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.
His branches will spread, and he will be like an olive tree laden with fruit; his fragrance will be like Lebanon.
They will return and settle beneath his shelter; they will live and be filled to intoxication with grain. His memorial will blossom like a vine, like Lebanon’s wine.

relationship: close praise with song and lyre
rationale: Both command singing and instrumental praise to the Lord and explicitly name the lyre among its means.
source_text: Ascribe greatness to His name and give thanks with His praise, with songs of lips and lyres; and thus you will say in thanksgiving:

target_units.text: Shout to God, all the earth; sing and exult and make music.
Make music to the Lord with a lyre, with a lyre and the sound of a psalm.
With hammered trumpets and the sound of a horn trumpet, shout before the King, the Lord.

relationship: close affirmation that all God's works are very good
rationale: Sirach declares all the Lord's works very good; Genesis records that same evaluation of all that God had made.
source_text: “All the Lord’s works are very good, and every command will come to pass at its time. One cannot say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For everything will be sought at its time.

target_units.text: And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning: a sixth day.

relationship: related goodness of divine works at their proper time
rationale: Sirach adds that each command and work has its time; Ecclesiastes likewise says God makes everything beautiful in its time and that His works endure.
source_text: “All the Lord’s works are very good, and every command will come to pass at its time. One cannot say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For everything will be sought at its time.

target_units.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put the age in their hearts, so that human beings may not find out the work God has done from beginning to end.
I knew that there is no good for them except to rejoice and do good during one’s life.
Moreover, whenever a person eats and drinks and sees good in all his toil, this is God’s gift.
I knew that everything God has done will endure for ever. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing taken from it; God has done this so that people may fear before Him.

relationship: close divine arrest of water
rationale: Sirach describes water standing like a heap at God's word; the Exodus song likewise describes waters standing firm as a wall by the breath of His wrath. The images and expression of agency differ.
source_text: At His word water stood like a heap, and at the utterance of His mouth came reservoirs of water.

target_units.text: And by the breath of Thy wrath the water parted; the waters stood fast as a wall; the waves stood fast in the midst of the sea.

relationship: narrative counterpart of water standing in a mass
rationale: Sirach recalls water standing like a heap; the Jordan crossing likewise has incoming water standing in one mass while Israel crosses. It supplies another concrete water-crossing setting without identifying Sirach's event exclusively.
source_text: At His word water stood like a heap, and at the utterance of His mouth came reservoirs of water.

target_units.text: The people set out from their tents to cross the Jordan, and the priests lifted up the ark of the covenant of the Lord ahead of the people.

As the priests carrying the ark of the covenant entered the Jordan and the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord dipped into the edge of the Jordan’s water—the Jordan was overflowing its whole bank, as in the days of wheat harvest—

the waters coming down from above stood. One mass stood very, very far away, as far as the region of Kiriath-jearim. The water flowing down descended into the Sea of Arabah, the Salt Sea, until it failed completely. The people stood opposite Jericho.

The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the Lord stood on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All the sons of Israel crossed on dry ground until the whole people had finished crossing the Jordan.

relationship: close effective divine good pleasure
rationale: Sirach locates God's good pleasure in His command; the psalm likewise says He does everything He wills throughout creation. Sirach additionally denies diminution of His salvation.
source_text: In His command is all His good pleasure, and no one can diminish His salvation.

target_units.text: Everything the Lord willed, He did, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all the deeps.

relationship: close all human deeds visible to God
rationale: Sirach places all flesh's works before God's eyes; the psalm likewise describes Him seeing every inhabitant and understanding all their deeds.
source_text: The works of all flesh are before Him, and nothing can be hidden from His eyes.

target_units.text: From heaven the Lord looked down; He saw all the sons of men.
From His prepared dwelling place He looked upon all who inhabit the earth.
He formed their hearts individually; He understands all their deeds.

relationship: related comprehensive divine knowledge across time
rationale: Sirach says God observes everything from age to age without surprise; Isaiah describes His announcing events before they happen and fulfilling His counsel.
source_text: From age to age He has looked upon everything, and nothing is astonishing before Him.

target_units.text: Remember the former things from eternity, for I am God, and there is none besides Me,
announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’

relationship: related affirmation of purposeful creation
rationale: Sirach says all things were created for their uses; Wisdom likewise says God created all things to exist and calls created things life-preserving, rather than repeating Sirach's precise formulation.
source_text: One cannot say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For all things have been created for their uses.

target_units.text: For He created all things that they might exist, and the created things of the world are life-preserving; there is no poison of destruction in them, nor is Hades’ dominion upon the earth.

relationship: shared river image for divine blessing
rationale: Sirach describes blessing covering like a river; Isaiah says obedience would have made the people's peace like a river and righteousness like a sea wave. Isaiah's statement is expressly conditional.
source_text: His blessing covered like a river and drenched dry land like a flood.

target_units.text: If you had listened to My commands, your peace would have become like a river and your righteousness like a sea wave.

relationship: related brine imagery for divine judgment
rationale: Sirach recalls waters changed into brine in an account of wrath; the psalm describes fruitful land becoming brine because of its inhabitants' wickedness. The transformed materials differ.
source_text: So nations will inherit His wrath, as when He turned waters into brine.

target_units.text: He made rivers a wilderness and outlets of waters thirst,
a fruitful land brine, because of the wickedness of those inhabiting it.

relationship: close straight divine ways with opposed human outcomes
rationale: Both call God's ways straight while distinguishing the righteous person's response from the impious person's failure within those same ways.
source_text: His ways are straight for the holy, but likewise stumbling blocks for the lawless.

target_units.text: Who is wise and will understand these things, or discerning and will recognize them? For the Lord’s ways are straight; the righteous will walk in them, but the impious will grow weak in them.

relationship: parallel creation's different effects upon righteous and unrighteous
rationale: Sirach distinguishes good things for the good and evils for sinners; Wisdom likewise describes creation serving punishment for the unrighteous and benefit for those trusting God.
source_text: Good things were created for the good from the beginning, and likewise evil things for sinners.

target_units.text: For creation, serving Thee who made it, strains itself for punishment against the unrighteous and relaxes itself for benefit on behalf of those who trust in Thee.

relationship: related enumeration of material provisions for life
rationale: Sirach's necessities include water, wheat, vine produce, oil, honey and iron; Deuteronomy's good-land description likewise names those resources. Neither list reproduces the other completely.
source_text: The first necessities for human life are water, fire, iron, salt, fine wheat flour, milk, honey, the blood of the grape, oil, and clothing.

target_units.text: For the Lord your God brings you into a good and spacious land, where are torrents of water and springs of the depths, flowing through the plains and through the hills;
a land of wheat and barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey,
a land wherein you shall eat your bread without poverty, and shall lack nothing; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you shall mine copper.
And you shall eat and be filled, and bless the Lord your God upon the good land which He has given you.

relationship: close beneficial provisions becoming harmful according to recipients
rationale: Sirach says life's provisions are good for the godly but become evils for sinners; Wisdom likewise contrasts creation's beneficial service with its punitive action, in the context of nourishment.
source_text: All these are good for the godly, but likewise will turn into evils for sinners.

target_units.text: For creation, serving Thee who made it, strains itself for punishment against the unrighteous and relaxes itself for benefit on behalf of those who trust in Thee.
Therefore at that time also, changing into all things, it served Thy gift that nourishes all, according to the desire of those in need,
so that Thy sons whom Thou didst love, Lord, might learn that it is not the production of fruits that nourishes a human being, but Thine utterance that preserves those who trust in Thee.

relationship: narrative example of fire and hail as judgment
rationale: Sirach names fire and hail among instruments of retribution; Exodus narrates the Lord sending both in the Egyptian plague, while distinguishing Goshen.
source_text: Fire, hail, famine, and death—all these were created for retribution;

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and there shall be hail throughout all the land of Egypt, upon men, and upon livestock, and upon every plant upon the earth.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven. The Lord sent thunder and hail, and fire ran over the earth. The Lord rained hail upon all the land of Egypt.
There was hail, with fire flaming amid the hail. The hail was very, very abundant, such as had never been in Egypt since a nation came to be there.
Throughout Egypt the hail struck people and livestock. It struck every plant in the plains and shattered all the trees there.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the sons of Israel were, was there no hail.

relationship: close beasts' teeth and sword as punitive threats
rationale: Both explicitly name beasts' teeth and the sword among divine punishments; Sirach additionally names scorpions and vipers.
source_text: the teeth of beasts, scorpions, vipers, and a sword exacting retribution upon the ungodly to their destruction.

target_units.text: I will gather evils against them, and spend My arrows upon them.

They shall waste away with hunger, and be devoured by birds, and suffer incurable backward-bending spasms; I will send against them the teeth of wild beasts, with the fury of things that crawl upon the ground.
Without, the sword shall bereave them; and from the inner chambers, terror: the young man together with the maiden, the nursing child with the aged elder.

relationship: parallel elemental forces obeying God's word
rationale: Sirach says the described punitive forces remain prepared and obey God's word; the psalm likewise describes fire, hail and other elements fulfilling His word.
source_text: They will rejoice in His command and be prepared upon the earth for their uses; at their times they will not transgress His word.”

target_units.text: Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps,
fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind—all fulfilling His word,

relationship: related considered instruction committed to writing
rationale: Sirach introduces teaching left in writing after reflection; the account of Ecclesiastes likewise describes instruction and the search for words written in uprightness and truth.
source_text: Therefore from the beginning I stood firm, reflected, and left this in writing:

target_units.text: Besides becoming wise, Ecclesiastes also taught the people knowledge; and an ear will trace out an orderly arrangement of proverbs.
Ecclesiastes sought much to find words of delight and something written in uprightness, words of truth.

relationship: close divine provision at the proper time
rationale: Sirach promises every need supplied at its proper hour; the psalm likewise describes creatures waiting for food at the right time and receiving goodness from God's hand.
source_text: “All the Lord’s works are good, and He will supply every need at its proper hour.

target_units.text: All wait for Thee to give them food at the right time.
When Thou givest to them, they will gather; when Thou openest Thy hand, all things will be filled with goodness.

relationship: close goodness evaluated in its proper time
rationale: Sirach says everything proves good at its time rather than allowing a simple worse-than comparison; Ecclesiastes similarly says God makes everything beautiful in its time.
source_text: One cannot say, ‘This is worse than that,’ for everything will prove good at its time.”

target_units.text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put the age in their hearts, so that human beings may not find out the work God has done from beginning to end.

relationship: close wholehearted blessing of God's name
rationale: Sirach calls for blessing the Lord's name with all heart and mouth; the psalm likewise calls the soul and all within it to bless His holy name.
source_text: And now sing hymns with all your heart and mouth, and bless the Lord’s name.

target_units.text: Of David. Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, His holy name.
Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all His repayments:
